synopsis: LEON replaces latent-world-model transition stacks with learned observable updates combining a shared, context-modulated operator basis and additive forcing. Its contribution concerns how future features are predicted while preserving each host policy’s prediction target and action interface. Reported LIBERO performance improves in VLA-JEPA, while matched LaWAM results remain slightly below baseline overall. Controlled dynamical-system experiments support the proposed inductive bias but do not establish exact Koopman dynamics in robot representations. [E02, E04, E09, E11, E16]

problem.text: The paper separates transition realization from the choice of predictive representation and the way predictions influence policy. It asks whether explicitly organizing latent changes as context-dependent evolution improves prediction and downstream control. The authors argue that Transformer predictors can learn temporal regularities, but their token-interaction architecture leaves the evolution law implicit; this is an inductive-bias argument, not an expressive-capacity limitation.

contributions.text: Introduces transition realization as an independent architectural variable and tests complete transition replacement while retaining the host WAM’s prediction and policy interfaces.
Develops context-modulated operator propagation in learned observable coordinates, with a shared operator basis and a complementary additive branch.
Combines two policy-coupling settings with controlled extrapolation and branch-intervention experiments to examine both downstream effectiveness and the proposed mechanism.

inputs: Current visual-state tokens, using V-JEPA representations in VLA-JEPA or projected DINOv3 features in LaWAM. [E05, E06]
VLM-produced timestep-specific latent-action tokens or a policy-predicted global latent-action vector. [E05, E06]
outputs: Predicted future V-JEPA representations or horizon DINO features. [E05, E06]
Executed actions are generated by the retained host action head; LEON itself outputs latent predictions. [E05, E06]

steps.name: Map state tokens to observables
steps.detail: A learned map converts each 1024-dimensional transition-state token into 768 observable coordinates in both implementations.

steps.name: Construct transition context
steps.detail: VLA-JEPA uses same-timestep visual-to-action cross-attention and an action-token summary. LaWAM combines each observable with the global latent action through a per-patch MLP.

steps.name: Modulate and apply the evolution operator
steps.detail: Context predicts coefficients over shared rank-one operator components. Their weighted sum, plus a diagonal baseline, acts multiplicatively on the current observable.

steps.name: Add forcing and compose layers
steps.detail: A context-dependent additive term complements operator propagation. A scaled residual update and learned readout produce the next layer’s representation; retained normalization and output projections produce the host prediction target.

steps.name: Preserve host coupling
steps.detail: The replacements use eight layers in VLA-JEPA and twelve in LaWAM. They add no visual–visual or cross-timestep attention in VLA-JEPA and no patch–patch attention in LaWAM; LaWAM’s frozen DINOv3 features already contain global context.

training.text: VLA-JEPA retains future-state prediction and flow-matching action objectives. LaWAM retains latent-action distillation, horizon-feature supervision and conditional action learning. LEON adds neither a prediction target nor a separate transition-pretraining stage.

inference.text: In VLA-JEPA, predicted futures are not consumed by the action generator at inference. LEON influences control through representations learned with predictive supervision.

In LaWAM, the policy predicts a latent action, LEON predicts its horizon feature, and the action expert consumes that prediction together with current visual features. This is direct predictive conditioning, without a described candidate-action search.

equations.expression: ṡ = f₀(s) + Σⱼ uⱼfⱼ(s); ḣ = (G₀ + Σⱼ uⱼGⱼ)h
equations.explanation: Equations (4)–(6) motivate shared operator components using control-affine physical dynamics. The finite-dimensional representation requires an invariant observable span. LEON adopts the modulation principle with learned context; it does not establish that invariant-span assumption for WAM features.

equations.expression: A(ξ) = D + U Diag(α(ξ)) Vᵀ; A(ξ) − D ∈ span{B₁,…,Bᵣ}
equations.explanation: Equations (11)–(12): D is a diagonal baseline, and Bₖ = pₖqₖᵀ are shared rank-one components. The factor width r bounds the dimension of context-dependent operator variation, not the rank of the complete operator including D.

equations.expression: hᵢ = φ(yᵢ); ξᵢ = C(hᵢ,Z); h̃ᵢ = hᵢ + η[A(ξᵢ)hᵢ + b(ξᵢ)]
equations.explanation: Equations (8)–(10) define observable mapping, conditioning and residual evolution. η scales the update. Because context depends on the observable, the complete mapping can be nonlinear, and additive forcing need not represent a purely external physical input.

results.setting: VLA-JEPA transition replacement; four-suite closed-loop evaluation. Baseline values are reproduced from prior reports.
results.comparison: VLA-JEPA averages 97.2%; improvement is 1.85 percentage points.
results.interpretation: Reported policy success improves across all four suites. The comparison does not include uncertainty estimates.

results.setting: Seven perturbation families using the reported benchmark protocol.
results.comparison: VLA-JEPA: 79.5%. Gains include camera +2.9, lighting +3.3, background +4.4, noise +2.3 and layout +2.6 percentage points.
results.interpretation: Robustness gains concentrate in visual and environmental changes; robot-state and language perturbations do not share the advantage.

results.setting: Matched four-task training and evaluation on Lift Pot, Beat Block Hammer, Dump Bin Bigbin and Hanging Mug.
results.comparison: Retrained LaWAM: 84.50% under each condition and overall.
results.interpretation: Full replacement preserves near-baseline aggregate performance, with a clean-condition gain and randomized-condition loss. The published model trained on the full task mixture is a separate reference.

results.setting: Training within a bounded amplitude range; testing unseen amplitudes under unchanged linear dynamics.
results.interpretation: Adaptive structure improves this physical-fidelity diagnostic even though the fixed model has more exact scale equivariance. These are dynamical prediction measurements.

results.setting: Eight individual or joint length-and-damping shifts.
results.value: Fixed and Adaptive Koopman each achieve the lowest error in four settings.
results.comparison: At least one structured predictor outperforms the Transformer in every setting.
results.interpretation: This prose-supported ranking avoids ambiguous concatenated cells. Terminal error is distinct from the separate cumulative rollout metric used for regime analysis.

results.setting: Paired condition swaps with symmetric averaging over ten seeds; Transformer and residual MLP parameter budgets match the full structured model.
results.metric: Trajectory RMSE, swap penalty and condition retrieval
results.value: Full structured: matched RMSE 0.08434, cross-condition RMSE 0.24944, swap penalty 0.16510, retrieval 81.4%.
results.interpretation: Accurate matched predictions and condition retrieval support functional conditioning. A large swap penalty alone would not establish prediction quality.

results.setting: Post-hoc removal of branches from the same trained structured model; OOD rollout means over ten seeds.
results.metric: RMSE relative to the complete model
results.interpretation: Both branches are used, with greater sensitivity to operator removal. This intervention does not measure the performance of separately retrained reduced models.

limitations.text: The authors explicitly caution that controlled-system results do not imply an exact Koopman description of learned WAM representations. The pendulum advantage also weakens after trajectories cross into continuous rotation.

WAM replacement changes a complete transition stack, including token-interaction structure. Without matched WAM parameter budgets or component ablations, the policy gains cannot be assigned specifically to the shared basis or forcing branch.

Published LIBERO comparisons have weaker attribution than the explicitly matched LaWAM retraining. Robot benchmark tables provide no seed variance or confidence intervals; physical-hardware deployment is not reported.

reproduction.text: Reconstruct the host interfaces and objectives with observable width 768, transition width 1024 and operator factor width 96. Use eight layers with residual scale 0.35 for VLA-JEPA, or twelve with scale 0.10 for LaWAM.

The supplied note leaves important implementation and experimental details unstated, including exact map/fusion architectures, optimizer schedules, training-data quantities, prediction horizons, compute and WAM evaluation seed counts. References to original configurations are insufficient for standalone reproduction.

A focused mechanism test would reproduce the parameter-matched driven oscillator, then compare post-hoc knockouts with independently retrained branch ablations. No code was inspected and no experiments were reproduced in this reading.

reasoning.text: The snapshot is reasonable at the contribution level: LEON is a latent-transition module evaluated within two inherited policy couplings, so a single complete-model architecture quadrant is not established. Context-modulated operator evolution supports Other mechanisms; the paper proposes neither inverse-dynamics action extraction nor joint future/action generation. The JEPA subcategory applies specifically to the VLA-JEPA integration, while LaWAM predicts DINO features. Joint training alone would not justify One Model.

discussionQuestions: Do WAM gains survive parameter-matched comparisons that separately vary operator structure and token mixing? [E05, E06, E08]
Does improved future-feature accuracy predict action success differently under representation-mediated and policy-facing coupling? [E05, E06]
Would retrained branch ablations preserve the contribution ordering observed in post-hoc oscillator knockouts? [E15]

evidence.location: PDF p. 2, Section 1; PDF p. 4, Section 3.1, Eq. (3)
evidence.detail: The paper distinguishes representation, prediction–policy coupling and transition realization, and frames the intervention as changing the conditional latent-transition architecture.
Control-affine dynamics yield shared generator components; a finite observable representation assumes an invariant span. Learned WAM context replaces explicit physical-control coefficients.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 4–5, Section 3.2, Eqs. (7)–(12) and Transition composition
evidence.detail: Defines observables, state-dependent context, residual operator-plus-forcing updates, diagonal baseline, rank-one basis factorization and learned readout.

Specifies eight replacement layers, 1024-to-768 mapping, same-timestep action cross-attention, absent visual/time attention and retained action head; predicted futures are not inference-time action inputs.
Specifies twelve replacement layers, frozen globally contextualized DINOv3 features, per-patch latent-action conditioning and future-feature input to the retained action expert.
